title: JRE 2240 - Roger Avary & Quentin Tarantino
guestBio: This episode is brought to you by The Farmer's Dog. Get 50% off your first box by heading to http://thefarmersdog.com/rogan today!
tldr: The Pulp Fiction origin story in detail: how Tarantino and Avary divided the writing, the specific literary and cinematic influences on the screenplay's structure, and Avary's underacknowledged contribution to the film's architecture

Hollywood in the early 1990s as a genuinely permissive creative environment: why studios were willing to fund formally experimental films with explicit content and how that ecosystem disappeared over the following decade

Tarantino's theory of cinematic violence: his philosophical framework for why violence in film functions differently from violence in reality, and why he thinks his critics fundamentally misunderstand what he's doing
The writing partnership between Tarantino and Avary: how their collaboration worked, how it fractured, what each took from the relationship, and how they think about the films they made together now
Tarantino's ten-film retirement plan: why he set the limit, how close he is to it, and what he wants to do after he stops making films - including his ambitions in other creative forms
The streaming era's impact on theatrical cinema: both filmmakers' arguments about what the collapse of the mid-budget adult drama has done to the overall health of film as an art form
recap:
Joe Rogan sits down with Quentin Tarantino and Roger Avary, the writing duo behind Pulp Fiction, for a conversation that is essentially a master class in 1990s American cinema delivered by the two people who made some of its most important films.

Tarantino is a legendary interview subject - his enthusiasm for film history is genuine and almost overwhelming, and he has opinions about everything from shot composition to distribution models to why certain actors are undervalued. Avary, who has never gotten quite the credit his writing contribution to Pulp Fiction deserved, is an equally fascinating presence, and having both of them together gives the conversation a texture you rarely get.

The Pulp Fiction origin story is detailed and entertaining. They talk about how the screenplay evolved, the specific influences - short story collections, crime novels, the rhythms of B-movies they grew up watching - and how they divided the writing labor. Avary's contribution to the structure of the film is more substantial than most people realize, and he articulates it clearly here. Joe is a genuine film nerd and his questions are specific and good.

Hollywood in the early 1990s was a genuinely different environment, and both men are eloquent about what made it possible to make something as strange and violent and formally experimental as Pulp Fiction and have it become a mainstream phenomenon. The studios were trying different things, independent film had real momentum, and there was appetite for cinema that wasn't purely commercial. They're both a little melancholy about how thoroughly that has changed.

Violence in cinema is discussed with the seriousness it deserves. Tarantino has thought about this more carefully than his critics credit - he has a theory about what cinematic violence does and doesn't do to audiences and he's articulate about it. Joe engages with the question honestly rather than just validating the auteur's self-assessment.

Tarantino's retirement plans come up. He has said for years that he intends to make ten films and stop, and he's getting close to that number. He talks about why the limit feels right to him and what he wants to do after. Avary has his own projects and they talk about how their creative paths have diverged and occasionally converged since the 1990s.

The film industry today versus then closes out the conversation - the streaming era, the death of the mid-budget adult drama, and whether cinema as a theatrical experience can survive what it's been through.
